issues.legal_issue: Pending appeals concerning land rights do not become infructuous merely because consolidation operations occur when the law applicable to those operations does not affect the appeals and later rules operate prospectively.
material_facts: Appeals concerning rights in land were pending when consolidation operations began in the relevant villages.
The consolidation operations were completed before the later amendments that expanded the consequences for pending proceedings took effect.
The appellants filed no objections before the consolidation authorities.
The provisions applicable while the operations were underway did not stay or otherwise affect these appeals, and the later amendments applied prospectively.
issues.conclusion: The appeals had not become infructuous and could proceed to hearing.
issues.legal_principle: Under the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, as it applied during the consolidation operations, sections 5 and 12 did not affect these pending appeals where no objection had been filed; section 49, as then amended, did not bar their institution. The later amendments, including the amendments to sections 5 and 12, operated prospectively, and the later provisions did not apply to operations already closed. Accordingly, consolidation did not render the appeals infructuous.

predicates.land_rights_appeal_pending: A party had an appeal pending concerning the determination of rights in land.
predicates.consolidation_law_during_operations_left: The law in force during the consolidation process did not stay or otherwise affect the pending appeal.
predicates.consolidation_operations_closed_before_l: The consolidation process had ended before later rules expanding the effect of consolidation on pending land-rights proceedings applied.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerning land rights remains unaffected under the rules in force during consolidation and the process ends before later stay rules apply, the appeal is not rendered infructuous.

issues.legal_issue: A common judgment disposing of separate suits does not make a final adjudication in one suit a bar to appeals arising from other suits when the adjudications involve different parties or different matters.
material_facts: Twelve suits concerned different sets of plots and were tried together because they raised similar issues.
The suits were disposed of by a common judgment, but separate decrees were prepared for them.
Three appeals involving a defendant who was not a party to the other suits were dismissed for default; the remaining appeals were decided on their merits.
The Board of Revenue dismissed the later appeals as barred by the finality of the three dismissals, although those dismissals concerned different parties and different plots.
issues.conclusion: The Board of Revenue was wrong to hold that the appeals were barred by res judicata; the appeals were allowed and remanded for further hearing and decision.
issues.legal_principle: Res judicata requires that the previous adjudication have been between the same parties and concern the same matter. A common judgment resolving several separate suits ordinarily amounts to as many judgments as there are suits. The Court relied on Badri Narayan Singh v. Kamdeo Prasad Singh, (1962) 3 S.C.R. 759.

predicates.appeal_challenging_res_judicata_dismissa: A party appealed a decision dismissing its case on the ground that an earlier adjudication barred it.
predicates.prior_adjudication_involved_different_pa: The earlier adjudication was between parties different from those in the proceeding under appeal.
predicates.prior_adjudication_concerned_different_s: The earlier adjudication concerned a different subject matter from the proceeding under appeal.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a dismissal based on an earlier adjudication that involved different parties or a different subject matter, the appeal is not barred by res judicata.
